s: Declarative container orchestration: schedule workloads, heal failures, roll deploys - the de-facto compute substrate for microservices.
w: A control plane reconciles desired state (Deployments) with reality: containers packed onto nodes respecting resource requests/limits, restarted when unhealthy, rescheduled when nodes die. Services give stable virtual IPs; HPA scales replicas on metrics; rolling updates surge new pods while retiring old. etcd stores cluster state.
use: Batch + serving mixed on one fleet with bin-packing efficiency
Self-healing requirements: node dies, pods relocate automatically
Portability across clouds/on-prem (cluster API is the same everywhere)
avoid: Two-service startups - a PaaS or single VM is cheaper than operating clusters
Truly serverless-shaped spiky loads (functions fit better)
Stateful naive lifts - databases need operators/PVC planning, not just Deployments

props.resource_requests: CPU/memory reserved per pod drives scheduling

size.rps_per_instance: Depends entirely on pods; cluster overhead ~3 control-plane nodes

pat.d: Mesh/logging agents join every pod automatically.
Two Deployment sets flipped by selector change - instant rollback.
Namespaces + ResourceQuotas partition teams so one cannot starve others.

pits: No requests/limits -> noisy neighbors and evictions; mandate QoS classes org-wide
etcd degradation cascades cluster-wide - monitor fsync latency, keep it on fast SSDs
YAML sprawl - adopt GitOps (Argo/Flux) or drown in kubectl history
tips: Explain reconciliation loop plainly - it's the interview core: desired vs actual, controllers converge
HPA discussion: scale on RPS vs CPU; CPU lags traffic, leading indicators better for bursty APIs
